blocks.text: Polyatomic ions are the ions composed of more than one type of atoms. Their formal charge is the net charge on them which is calculated based on the number of electrons in their valence shells after the formation of bonds. With the exception of ammonium ion (NH₄⁺), these ions mostly carry a negative charge, for example the carbonate (CO₃²⁻), sulfate (SO₄²⁻), and nitrate (NO₃³⁻) ions. In some polyatomic ions, the central atom violates the octet rule by expanding its electron density to the higher orbitals. These are said to have expanded octets. Some prominent examples are SO₄²⁻, ClO₄⁻, PO₄³⁻.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book writes nitrate as NO₃³⁻. The nitrate ion carries one negative charge: N (+5) + 3 × O (−2) = −1, so it is NO₃⁻.

blocks.alt: Lewis structure of the sulfate ion in square brackets with charge 2- at the top right. Sulfur is in the centre with double bonds to the oxygen atoms above and below it and single bonds to the oxygen atoms on the left and right. Each double-bonded oxygen has two lone pairs and each single-bonded oxygen has three lone pairs. The words 'sulfate ion' are written inside the brackets.
blocks.caption: Lewis structure of the sulfate ion (original drawing after the structure printed beside the text in the textbook).

blocks.text: From the Lewis structures of SO₄²⁻, we can calculate the number of electrons around the central S atom.
The number of electrons in the valence shell of S atom can be calculated as:

blocks.latex: \text{No of valence electrons} = 2 \times (\text{double bond electrons}) + 2 \times (\text{single bond electrons})
blocks.text_alt: No of valence electrons = 2 × (double bond electrons) + 2 × (single bond electrons)

blocks.text: Thus, S has 12 electrons in its valence shell and it exceeds the octet by 4 electrons. The expansion of octet is caused by the involvement of the d orbital in bonding, which can accommodate the extra electrons. The following electronic configuration of native S(0) atom shows that it has two unpaired electrons in the p orbitals. The presence of d-orbital allows this configuration to extend to 4 unpaired electrons by the transfer of one electron from the 3p pair. It explains not only the variable oxidation states of S, but also the possibility of accepting extra electrons in its d orbital.
book_errors: 4 unpaired electrons by the transfer of one electron from the 3p pair

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The text and the boxes printed below disagree. Moving one 3p electron into 3d gives four unpaired electrons (3s² 3p³ 3d¹), the state used in SO₂. The printed boxes show six unpaired electrons (3s¹ 3p³ 3d²: one 3s electron is also promoted), which is the state needed for the six bonds of sulfur in SO₄²⁻.

blocks.alt: Two rows of orbital boxes for sulfur, each with one 3s box, three 3p boxes and five 3d boxes. Top row: 3s has a pair of opposite arrows, 3p has one pair and two single up arrows, 3d is empty. Bottom row: 3s has one up arrow, each 3p box has one up arrow, and the first two 3d boxes have one up arrow each.
blocks.caption: Electron boxes of sulfur: 3s, 3p and 3d orbitals before and after promotion of electrons (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: In the same way, we can calculate the number of valence electrons around the central iodine atom in the tri-iodide ion. The Lewis structure of the ion is given by:

blocks.alt: Lewis structure of the tri-iodide ion: three iodine atoms in a line, I-I-I, joined by two single bonds. Each iodine atom carries three lone pairs. The structure is in square brackets with a minus charge at the top right.
blocks.caption: Lewis structure of the tri-iodide ion, [I3]- (original drawing after the structure printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: The number of valence electrons of the central atom can be calculated as follows,

blocks.latex: \text{No of valence electrons} = 2 \times (\text{no. of single bond electrons}) + 2 \times (\text{no. of lone pairs})
blocks.text_alt: No of valence electrons = 2 × (no. of single bond electrons) + 2 × (no. of lone pairs)

blocks.text: The central iodine atom in tri-iodide ion (I₃⁻) has 10 electrons in the valence shell and the octet expands by two electrons.
